name: English (Scotland)
variety: Scottish Standard English, the English of educated speakers in the Central Belt (Edinburgh and Glasgow); not Scots
sources: Wells, J. C. (1982). Accents of English. Volume 2: The British Isles. Cambridge University Press.
Abercrombie, David (1979). The accents of Standard English in Scotland. In Aitken and McArthur (eds.), Languages of Scotland. Edinburgh: Chambers.
Aitken, A. J. (1981). The Scottish Vowel-length Rule. In Benskin and Samuels (eds.), So Meny People Longages and Tonges. Edinburgh.

Scobbie, James M.; Hewlett, Nigel; Turk, Alice (1999). Standard English in Edinburgh and Glasgow: the Scottish Vowel Length Rule revealed. In Foulkes and Docherty (eds.), Urban Voices: Accent Studies in the British Isles. London: Arnold.
Stuart-Smith, Jane (2004). Scottish English: phonology. In Schneider et al. (eds.), A Handbook of Varieties of English, volume 1. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.

Scobbie, James M.; Gordeeva, Olga B.; Matthews, Benjamin (2007). Scottish English speech acquisition. In McLeod (ed.), The International Guide to Speech Acquisition. Clifton Park: Thomson Delmar Learning.
Cruttenden, Alan (1997). Intonation. 2nd edition. Cambridge University Press.
Mayo, Catherine; Aylett, Matthew; Ladd, D. Robert (1997). Prosodic transcription of Glasgow English: an evaluation study of GlaToBI. In Proceedings of the ESCA Workshop on Intonation, Athens.
contrasts: rhotic: /r/ is pronounced in all positions, and there are no centring diphthongs and no separate long vowels of the RP kind (card [kard], beard [bird])
FOOT and GOOSE are one phoneme /ʉ/ (pull = pool, full = fool)
TRAP, BATH and PALM are one phoneme /a/ (Sam = psalm, ant = aunt); there is no TRAP-BATH split
LOT, CLOTH and THOUGHT are one phoneme /ɔ/ (cot = caught)
FOOT and STRUT are separate, as in the south of England (/ʉ/ versus /ʌ/)
FACE and GOAT are monophthongs /e/ and /o/
more vowel contrasts before /r/ than in other accents: NORTH versus FORCE (horse [ɔr] versus hoarse [or]), and for many speakers three NURSE vowels (fir [ɪr], fern [ɛr], fur [ʌr])
/ʍ/ versus /w/ (which versus witch) and /x/ versus /k/ (loch versus lock)
vowel length is not phonemic but follows the Scottish Vowel Length Rule, which creates near-minimal pairs at morpheme boundaries (brood versus brewed, tide versus tied)
allophony: Scottish Vowel Length Rule: /i/, /ʉ/ and /ai/ are long before /r/, before the voiced fricatives /v ð z ʒ/ and at the end of a morpheme, and short elsewhere, also before voiced stops, nasals and /l/ (leave long, lead short; agreed long, greed short; brewed long, brood short); for the other vowels the rule is weak or absent in the standard accent
the PRICE diphthong has two forms under the rule: short [ʌi] (tide, life, price) and long [ae] (tied, five, prize)
/r/ is an alveolar tap [ɾ] or a postalveolar or retroflex approximant [ɹ]; approximants are usual after vowels in middle-class speech, taps between vowels and after consonants; a trill is rare
KIT is lowered and centralised, close to [ë]; final unstressed happY is [e] or [i]
MOUTH is [ʌʉ], with a central rounded end
many speakers have merged the three NURSE vowels into a rhotic central vowel [əɾ] or [ɚ]
/p t k/ are less aspirated than in RP; /t/ is often a glottal stop after a vowel in urban speech
a vowel may be inserted in /rm/, /rl/ and /lm/ (film [ˈfɪləm], girl [ˈɡɪɾəl])
unstressed syllables have [ə], [ɪ] or [ʌ]; final unstressed commA is often [ʌ]
phonotactics: /r/ occurs before vowels, before consonants and at the end of words
/x/ occurs after vowels in Scottish words and names (loch, Buchan) and in a few loans
/ŋ/ does not begin a syllable; /h/ and /ʍ/ only begin a syllable
clusters as in other accents of English; /rl/, /rm/, /lm/ may be broken up by a vowel

stress.rule: As in other accents of English, with a few words stressed differently (for example final stress in verbs such as realise and advertise for some speakers).
stress.cues: pitch movement on accented syllables, duration, loudness and vowel quality

rhythm.vowel_reduction: strong, but with more full vowels in unstressed syllables than RP
rhythm.notes: Stressed vowels in closed syllables are short under the Vowel Length Rule, which gives disyllables a short first and longer second syllable. I know of no nPVI value for Scottish Standard English that I can cite.

length.notes: Vowel duration is set by the Scottish Vowel Length Rule and not by the vowel phoneme: there are no inherently long and short vowel classes. Scobbie, Hewlett and Turk (1999) found the rule to hold firmly for /i ʉ ai/.

intonation.declarative: Edinburgh: falling nuclear accent with a low end; Glasgow: statements commonly have a low accented syllable followed by a rise, with a high plateau or a slight fall at the end
intonation.yes_no_question: rise on and after the nucleus; in Glasgow the contour of questions is close to that of statements and the pitch range carries the difference
intonation.wh_question: falling in Edinburgh, rise or rise plus plateau in Glasgow
intonation.accent_shape: Edinburgh H* L (fall from the accented syllable); Glasgow L* H (low on the accented syllable, rise after it)
intonation.notes: Glasgow belongs to the group of northern British cities with rising statement tunes described by Cruttenden (1997); Mayo, Aylett and Ladd (1997) adapted ToBI to Glasgow English.

phonation: glottal replacement of /t/ after vowels in urban speech

problems: the Scottish Vowel Length Rule is modelled in part: /i/ and /ʉ/ are lengthened before voiced fricatives and before a pause, and PRICE takes its long form before vowels, voiced fricatives and at the end of a word; but morpheme boundaries inside a word are not seen, so brewed = brood, tied = tide, agreed has the vowel of greed
the short and the long PRICE diphthong share one formant file and differ only in duration; the language has [ʌi] against [ae]
/l/ is clear before vowels as in RP; Scottish /l/ is dark in all positions
/r/ before a vowel is an approximant and /r/ after a vowel is only a colouring of the vowel (the phoneme r/ has no sound of its own); taps are not used
TRAP (length 200) and BATH or PALM (length 220) keep a small length difference, and LOT and THOUGHT use different formant data, although each pair is one phoneme in this accent
there is no glottal replacement of /t/
the tunes are the default English ones: the rising statements of Glasgow are not available, and wh-questions get the rising question tune
good: rhotic, with r-coloured vowels, and NORTH [ɔr] kept apart from FORCE [or]
FOOT and GOOSE are both [ʉ]; FACE and GOAT are monophthongs; MOUTH is [ʌʉ]
the NURSE vowels are split by spelling into [ɪr], [ɛr] and [ʌr] (bird, fern, fur)
wh is voiceless [ʍ] and loch has [x]
KIT is centralised, happY is [e], and final unstressed schwa is [ʌ]

notes: The vowel list gives the nine stressed monophthongs of the basic Scottish system plus schwa; some speakers add RP-like contrasts (TRAP against PALM, LOT against THOUGHT, FOOT against GOOSE) in that order of frequency (Abercrombie 1979). [ʌi] and [ae] in the diphthong list are the two forms of PRICE. I give no formant or duration values because I cannot quote the published figures with confidence.
